 Key developments
 • Michigan party strife: Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign has asked his former primary opponent , Rep. Haley Stevens, to skip all campaign events in the race’s closing days, a source said. Their planned unity event Sunday may now likely exclude Stevens.
 • Rallies back on: President Donald Trump claimed he restored his weekend events in Kansas and Iowa because of requests from Republicans in those states. He rallied in Florida tonight for the second time in a week and warned the state’s Republicans not to get too confident.
 • Pressure campaign: A federal judge imposed an emergency order halting the Trump administration’s pressure tactics on election officials.
 • Alaska Senate race: Amid a federal investigation into ballot-stacking allegations in Alaska, Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola called the accusations “offensive.”

 Peltola calls election conspiracy allegations "offensive" amid federal investigation
 By Karina Tsui 
 Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a campaign rally at the Alaska Aviation Museum in Anchorage, Alaska, on October 30, 2026. 
 Justin Sullivan/Getty Images 
 Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola said she would be “happy to fire” her former campaign manager again after the ex-staffer alleged Peltola was aware of efforts to recruit a candidate with the same name as her Republican opponent to create confusion among voters.
 Peltola’s comments come after the New York Times on Wednesday published findings alleging that her team orchestrated a campaign to stack the ballot against her opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.
 In an exclusive interview with CNN affiliate KTUU Friday, Peltola said she had “honestly no idea” whether anyone on her campaign was involved in the alleged effort.
 “This is offensive to me on a number of different levels. First of all, this is Alaska; we’re not in the business of tricking each other up here,” Peltola told the outlet.
 She also pushed back against accusations from Republicans, saying: “Every single accusation that’s been made of me is a confession on their side.”
 “I think this is a real reflection on how deeply scared they are,” she added.
 Peltola said she was still learning the details of the federal investigation, which comes days before Election Day.

 Catch up: Judge orders halt on Trump's pressure tactics, Democrat unity wavers in Michigan
 By Xiaoqian Lin 
 Trina Thompson, nominated to be US District Judge for the Northern District of California, testifies before a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on February 16, 2022. 
 Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters 
 A federal judge has imposed a sweeping emergency order halting aggressive tactics employed by the Trump administration to pressure election officials.
 While the order is in place, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters from voter rolls, or halt ballot processing, said US District Judge Trina Thompson.
 Her opinion rebuked claims the administration has made that it can and will prosecute election officials for not doing enough to prevent illegal voting.
 More headlines from Friday evening:
 Trump rallies in Florida: In his second rally in a week in the red state, President Donald Trump warned Republicans not to get too confident ahead of Tuesday’s elections. He also said he thought that Friday’s rally would be the last one of his midterm blitz and claimed he restored his canceled weekend events in Iowa and Kansas because of requests from Republicans in those states.
 Alaska Senate race: At his Florida rally, Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche would make his own decision about a criminal probe into alleged ballot-stacking in Alaska. Trump previously made clear he was behind the DOJ preemptively filing a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the state’s Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses. Meanwhile, Alaskan voters weighed in on the controversy , with one telling CNN: “My obligation is to vote.”
 Michigan Democrat tensions: Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign has asked his former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens to stay away from campaign events in the final days of the midterms race, according to a source. The two had traded barbs on Friday, with El-Sayed saying Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago” after she called on him to denounce an outside group’s controversial advertisement. Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow urged Stevens to get behind El-Sayed, while Republican rival Mike Rogers accused him of antisemitism.
 CNN’s Eric Bradner, Tierney Sneed, Kit Maher, Aleena Fayaz, Tori B. Powell and Elise Hammond contributed reporting.

 Source: El-Sayed campaign asks Stevens to stay away from events in Senate race's final days
 By Eric Bradner 
 People attend a primary election night watch party with Rep. Haley Stevens, in Detroit, in August. 
 Emily Elconin/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign has asked his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, to skip all campaign events in the race’s closing days, a person familiar with the matter said.
 That means a planned Sunday show of unity — with El-Sayed and Stevens appearing at a Detroit church with South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the party’s most influential Black leaders — is now likely to exclude Stevens.
 It would have been her first time appearing alongside El-Sayed since their heated August primary. Politico first reported that the El-Sayed campaign had asked the congresswoman to stay away from events. Stevens did not immediately respond to a request for comment about her plans.
 The news comes after the two traded barbs Friday . In the morning, Stevens issued a statement aimed at pressuring El-Sayed into denouncing an outside group’s controversial advertisement that blames the United States’ foreign aid for Israel for Americans’ struggles with high costs. El-Sayed responded in a statement Friday night that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
 The war of words comes amid questions about how Jewish Democrats in Michigan will vote. El-Sayed is a vocal critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza and of the United States’ financial backing of Israel’s military. The American Israel Political Affairs Committee spent tens of millions of dollars attempting to defeat him during the August primary, but El-Sayed topped Stevens by less than a percentage point.
 State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who also ran in the Senate primary but dropped out four weeks before the election, was sharply critical of Stevens on CNN Friday night, casting her actions as disruptive to Democrats’ chances of defeating Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers and retaining a Senate seat that is crucial to the battle for majority control of the chamber next Tuesday.
 “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes,” McMorrow said.

 Judge imposes emergency order halting Trump's pressure campaign on election officials
 By Tierney Sneed 
 A federal judge imposed a sweeping emergency order halting various aggressive tactics employed by the Trump administration in recent days to pressure election officials across the country.
 “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” US District Judge Trina Thompson said in her opinion granting a temporary restraining order Friday evening.
 She said, while her order is in place, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters from voter rolls, or halt ballot processing.
 Thompson, who was appointed by President Joe Biden, is also blocking threats of criminal prosecutions against election officials from those agencies and said that the administration cannot take other actions that “threaten, intimidate or coerce” election officials to demand changes in ballot processing procedures on claims the voters are ineligible.
 Thompson’s opinion rebuked claims the administration has made for months that it can and will prosecute election officials for not doing enough to prevent illegal voting.

 President Donald Trump thought Friday’s rally would be the last of his midterm blitz, he told attendees in Daytona Beach, Florida.
 “I thought this was going to be my last one,” Trump said. “I thought this was it. I thought I could relax — 28 days in a row of this crap is … It’s a lot. My voice is about operating at about 49.2%.”
 Further explaining why weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas were canceled on Thursday and then restored to his schedule, Trump said he had questioned whether his presence would even matter.
 “They called me in Iowa, and they called me in Kansas, and they said, ‘Sir, would it be possible to do a little rally of about 50,000 people each?’ And I said, ‘Does it matter?’ They said, ‘We just want to make sure that we win.’”
 “So on Sunday, while you’re all watching football, I’ll be traveling in a very beautiful airplane to Iowa, to Kansas,” Trump said.
 “We have to be sure,” the president continued. “We do the rally. It’s very likely, so I’ll be doing that, and my son Eric will be watching, watching a beautiful football game or something.”
 Tonight was Trump’s 26th rally in October.

 Trump says Blanche will 'make own decision' about Alaska probe 
 1:13
 President Donald Trump said Friday that Attorney General Todd Blanche would make his own decision about whether Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola should be prosecuted — while making his own wishes very clear.
 “She should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. But he’s going to make his own decision. I’m not telling you. Todd, please make your own, right,” Trump said during a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, while alluding to the criminal probe into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a candidate intended to siphon votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
 Trump then told the crowd — which included Blanche — that that other candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, should also be prosecuted.
 “And so should the fake Dan Sullivan. He should be prosecuted. You know, he never campaigned one day. Did you know that, Mr. Attorney General? We have a great attorney general here. Really great guy. So, Mr. Attorney General, he never, he never went out and campaigned.”
 Trump claimed Daniel J. Sullivan tried to change his middle initial from “J” to “S,” before telling the audience “there’s much worse than that.”
 “Wait till you see,” he added.
 Last week, Trump made clear he was behind the Justice Department preemptively filing a lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses.
 “Well, I’m the one that said ‘do it,’” Trump told reporters last Friday.
 Blanche tried to walk back that assertion by saying in an interview days later that the Justice Department was conducting its own research, but declined to discuss his conversations with Trump, who had publicly raised the issue for months.

 "Bad things happen when you get too confident," Trump tells Florida Republicans
 By Kit Maher 
 President Donald Trump takes the stage during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena on October 30, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Florida. 
 Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump urged Florida Republicans to play from behind, warning them not to get too confident ahead of Tuesday’s elections.
 “You got to vote. Bad things happen when you get too confident, right? So let’s pretend they’re one point down,” Trump told a rally crowd in Daytona Beach.
 “It sounds a little negative, because they’re doing actually very well, but you have to go and vote,” he said, referring to GOP Sen. Ashley Moody and GOP Rep. Byron Donalds, who’s running for governor.
 “The ‘Free state of Florida’ is not going to send a communist to the Senate. You must elect Ashley Moody, who’s fantastic. I think you’re gonna be fine, but you got to go and vote,” Trump added.
 Trump has played two videos so far during tonight’s rally aimed at energizing his base — one seizing on controversial comments from some Democratic candidates and another mashing up news clips about illegal immigration.
 “We’re not going back,” Trump said. “That was no good, foreboding place. If Democrats ever get the chance to open the borders again, our nation will never be able to recover.”
 The rally was also interrupted by more than a few protesters within the first 30 minutes. At one point, Trump told one of them to “shut up,” adding, “What a loser! Get him out of here!”
 The crowd then chanted, “We love Trump!”

 Alaskan voters are reacting to Democrats’ alleged attempt to confuse them with a second Senate candidate named Dan Sullivan.

 The New York Times published an investigation Wednesday that found that staffers and lawyers for Alaska Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and other operatives aligned with the campaign spent months recruiting candidates they hoped could take votes away from the GOP Sullivan.

 Michigan GOP Senate nominee Rogers accuses rival El-Sayed of antisemitism
 By Eric Bradner 
 Mike Rogers, the Republican former congressman running for Michigan’s Senate seat, said Friday night on X that his Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign “has been based on vile racism and antisemitism.” He told those who backed El-Sayed’s former Democratic primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens that they have “a home with us.”
 Rogers’ comment comes after El-Sayed brushed off pressure from Stevens to denounce an outside group’s controversial advertisement criticizing the United States’ foreign aid for Israel.
 Rogers has been attempting to siphon Jewish Democratic votes away from El-Sayed, a progressive critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza and US spending bolstering Israel’s military. He has sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. 
 “I say today: if you are a Haley Stevens voter who rejects this bigoted and hateful candidate, you have a home with us. If you believe we can all work together to make housing affordable, improve education and, lower gas prices, you have a home with us,” he wrote.

 Trump arrives for second Florida rally in a week
 By Julia Benbrook in Daytona Beach, Florida
 President Donald Trump walks off Air Force One as he arrives at Daytona Beach International Airport on October 30, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Florida. 
 Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump has arrived in Florida, where he’ll be rallying supporters in Daytona Beach — the latest stop on his red-state blitz with just days before the midterms.
 It’s also his second rally in Florida in a week, after appearing in Fort Myers last Friday.
 The Republican National Committee believes this stop, and others, highlight that the GOP isn’t taking anything for granted this year, an official said.
 “The Sunshine State is Trump Country, and Floridians are fired up to rally with the President because they want more America First results,” the official said.
 Florida has trended very Republican in the Trump era. A New York Times/Siena poll released earlier this week showed that the Senate race here is not nearly as competitive as in some red states with margin-of-error races. GOP Sen. Ashley Moody led Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon by 6 points, 50-44% .
 The governor’s race was slightly closer, with GOP Rep. Byron Donalds at 48% and Democratic former Rep. David Jolly at 44%.

 El-Sayed brushes off former primary rival Stevens’ call to denounce controversial ad
 By Eric Bradner 
 Attendees holding signs cheer before Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed arrives to speak during a campaign rally at the UAW Local 600 union hall on Friday, Oct. 30, in Dearborn, Michigan. 
 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP 
 Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is brushing off a call from his former primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, to denounce a controversial advertisement criticizing the United States’ foreign aid for Israel.
 El-Sayed said in a statement Friday night that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
 His comment comes two days before they are scheduled to appear together at a Detroit church for a unity event — their first joint appearance since the August primary. El-Sayed is working to consolidate support among two groups that largely backed Stevens during the primary: Jewish and Black Democrats.
 El-Sayed also pointed out in his statement that in his narrow primary victory, he’d overcome tens of millions of dollars in spending by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee aimed at boosting Stevens.
 Hours earlier on Friday, Stevens released a statement of her own, lambasting El-Sayed for failing to sufficiently denounce an advertisement by the outside group Rebellion PAC, founded by leftist commentator Cenk Uygur. The ad features a couple at a grocery store, discussing how they can’t afford items like eggs “because we have to put that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.”
 El-Sayed’s statement Friday night said that his campaign “has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing: Skyrocketing gas prices, unaffordable groceries, and the inability to see a doctor.”
 “Now the stakes are even higher — defeating Trump’s hand-picked candidate, taking back the Senate, and defending our democracy,” El-Sayed said. “That should be the priority for all of us right now.”

 Multiple active lawsuits could have big implications for the midterms. Here's what to know
 By August Phillips 
 A woman casts her early vote at the Silverlake Community Church in Los Angeles on October 29, 2026. 
 David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images 
 As we enter the final weekend before Election Day , a flurry of legal activity concerning vote casting and counting integrity is adding another layer of unpredictability to a midterm cycle already full of surprises.
 Just today, we’ve gotten a decision in California concerning voter rolls and new developments in the Alaska Senate race saga concerning the multiple Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
 Here’s a rundown of what’s been happening in the courts today: 
 California-DOJ case: A federal appeals court rejected the Justice Department’s demand that election officials in California set aside some 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration claims the people who cast them could be noncitizens, but their evidence relies on a controversial data matching program.
 What the judges said: In a 2-1 ruling, the majority pointed to the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which says states are in charge of running elections while giving Congress the option to pass regulations. The dissenting judge called the request “a modest remedy—stopping California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens.”
 What’s next? The appeals court’s rejection of the DOJ lawsuit Friday sets up the possibility that President Donald Trump will now go to the US Supreme Court with the case.

 In Dearborn, Michigan — the US city with the largest Arab American community — some voters who cast their ballots for President Donald Trump in the past are rethinking their decisions.

 The voter said he supports El-Sayed regardless of his ethnicity or religion, because of his platform and promises to “keep our tax dollars for us.”

 DOJ asks judge to immediately segregate Alaska ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan
 By Tierney Sneed 
 In new filings Friday afternoon, the Trump administration requested that ballots immediately be segregated as part of its lawsuit targeting Alaska’s Senate election and the Justice Department asked the judge to fast-track its requests that Democrats turn over information about their efforts to recruit a spoiler candidate in the race.
 If there’s a vote for Daniel J. Sullivan, the Justice Department wants it to be set aside.
 The administration made the requests as the judge has set a quick timeline that could resolve the case by Monday.
 Judge Sharon Gleason is considering requests from Alaska election officials, Democrats and outside groups that she toss the DOJ’s lawsuit, which seeks to delay certification of the election if the incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses in order to investigate whether voter confusion caused his defeat.
 In response to Alaska’s arguments that the administration is not putting forward evidence that voters are being confused by the presence of the candidate Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot, the DOJ said that it was “common sense that a sham candidate on the ballot with the same name as the incumbent might confuse voters.”
 “The segregation of ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan constitutes a negligible further burden on Defendants,” the Justice Department request says.
 Alaska election officials had also noted that the administration had not spelled out how exactly it would be determined, if Sen. Sullivan lost, that voter confusion led to his defeat.
 “Defendants can take measures, including but not limited to the segregation of ballots, to ensure the integrity of Alaska’s elections results, and this Court can order them to do so,” DOJ said Friday afternoon.
 The administration also said the judge should order the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee and the campaign for Rep. Mary Peltola, the Sen. Sullivan’s Democratic challenger, to quickly comply with “tailored” discovery requests aimed at sussing out whether Sullivan’s candidacy was “frivolous or fraudulent.”
 Alaska’s Republican-led elections office — which tried to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot but was stopped by the state supreme court several months ago — agued that Daniel J.’s motives for running were irrelevant to the legal debate over whether the federal government has the legal right to interfere in certification.
 The DOJ said that the information it is seeking from the Democrats “strikes at the core of the United States’ claims.”

 Abdul El-Sayed condemned progressive streamer Hasan Piker’s comments comparing the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee’s canvassers door-knocking in the heavily Jewish West Bloomfield to “going to that like Klan KKK neighborhood to stump for like a Black candidate.”

 El-Sayed has long criticized Israel’s actions in Gaza and US foreign aid for Israel. He appeared with Piker, a strident pro-Palestinian commentator, at multiple events before the August Senate primary.

 White House deputy chief of staff calls Alaska Democrats’ alleged actions "repugnant"
 By Tori B. Powell 
 White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller attends a Halloween event at the White House on Thursday. 
 Finn Gomez/Getty Images 
 White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller called Alaska Democrats’ alleged attempt to confuse voters with a second Senate candidate named Dan Sullivan “a profound criminal act.”
 “It’s a criminal conspiracy to disenfranchise the voters and citizens of Alaska,” Miller told Fox News’ Will Cain.
 Last week, the Trump administration preemptively filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
 Miller told Cain it’s important “to understand the gravity of the matters being alleged and how seriously this is being taken by the US Department of Justice.”
 The lawsuit alleges a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could confuse voters and wants a court to potentially delay the certification of the election if the incumbent is defeated but would have won if “all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan” had “been cast instead for Senator Sullivan.”
 Miller maintained that the alleged actions from the Democrats are “repugnant” and claimed they are against the law.
 “To lie so casually, so repeatedly, so comfortably, it’s genuinely it’s sociopathic,” he said. “They lied again and again and again when everyone knows the truth.”
 However, legal experts say the findings from The New York Times investigation aren’t illegal and don’t give the DOJ’s lawsuit any more credence.
 CNN’s Tierney Sneed and Ethan Cohen contributed reporting.
